Typosquatting bets on your typo. Slopsquatting bets on your AI assistant. When a model invents a package that doesn't exist, an attacker registers the name and waits for install to run. Here's the kill chain, why your usual defenses miss it, and what actually stops it across npm, Composer, and pip.

Imagine a coding assistant just told you to run this:

pip install requests-oauth2-helper

It looks right. You asked for a clean way to attach OAuth2 tokens to your requests calls, and the name reads exactly like a package that would do that. The casing is idiomatic, the hyphenation matches the ecosystem, it sounds like fifty other real PyPI helpers. So you run it. Tests pass. You move on.

The problem is that requests-oauth2-helper never existed when the model learned to suggest it. The model made it up. And if an attacker was paying attention, that name isn't empty anymore.

That's slopsquatting: a supply chain attack that swaps the human typo at the heart of typosquatting for a machine hallucination. The term was coined by Seth Larson, Developer-in-Residence at the Python Software Foundation, and popularized by Andrew Nesbitt of Ecosyste.ms in 2025. It's a small idea with a nasty consequence: you don't have to fat-finger reqeusts anymore. Your AI will confidently hand you a fake package with a straight face, and you'll trust it more than your own typo.

Typosquatting needed your mistake. This one doesn't.

Typosquatting is old. You register expres next to express, python-dateutl next to python-dateutil, and you wait for someone's fingers to slip. It works, but it's a numbers game with thin odds. Most people spell express correctly. The attacker is fishing for the fraction of a percent who don't.

Slopsquatting removes that dependency on human error entirely. The developer types the name correctly, character for character, because they're copying it from a source they trust more than themselves right now: the assistant that just wrote the surrounding code. The mistake was already made upstream, by the model, and the human is faithfully reproducing it.

Here's the shift that matters. In typosquatting, the attacker guesses at what your fingers might slip into. In slopsquatting, the attacker doesn't guess at all. They read what the model actually outputs, at scale, and register the names that come up. The model is doing the target selection for them.

Why this works: hallucinations are frequent, and worse, they repeat

If model hallucinations were rare and random, slopsquatting would be a footnote. Register a fake name, wait forever, catch nobody. The reason this is a real threat is that neither of those things is true.

The scale first. A USENIX Security 2025 study, We Have a Package for You!, generated 576,000 code samples across 16 LLMs in Python and JavaScript and checked every package the models recommended. 19.7% of recommended packages didn't exist. That's not a rounding error at the edge of a benchmark. That's one in five. The study logged 205,474 distinct hallucinated package names. Commercial models were better behaved (at least 5.2% on average) and open-source models worse (at least 21.7%), but nobody was clean.

The scale would still be manageable if every hallucination were a unique snowflake, because an attacker can't register two hundred thousand names and would have no idea which ones anyone will ever see again. The killer finding is that hallucinations are reproducible. The researchers took 500 prompts that had produced a fake package and ran each one ten more times. 43% of the hallucinated packages came back every single time. 58% showed up in more than one run. Only 39% never reappeared.

Sit with that. Nearly half of these fabrications are stable model behavior, not noise. That flips the economics completely. An attacker doesn't need to register everything. They mine model output, keep the names that recur, and register the sticky ones. The reproducibility is the reconnaissance. The model tells them, over and over, exactly which fake name a future developer is most likely to be handed.

Warning
The names don't even have to look like real packages. Using Levenshtein distance, the same study found only 13% of hallucinated names were simple typos of real ones. About 38% had moderate similarity, and nearly half were highly dissimilar: fully fabricated, but still believable in the context of the code around them. That last bucket is the one that walks straight past typosquat detection, and we'll come back to why.

The kill chain, one step at a time

None of this is theoretical. It's a clean, repeatable sequence, and every link is something you've watched happen in a normal workday.

1. The model suggests an import. You ask for a feature. The assistant writes the code and reaches for a dependency that fits the shape of the problem. It emits a name. The name is invented, but it's grammatical: right ecosystem conventions, right casing, right "sounds like a thing that exists" energy.

2. You trust it because the name fits. This is the load-bearing step, and it's psychological, not technical. Confident AI output slides past your guard the same way a confident senior engineer's PR does. The name is idiomatic. Nothing about it pattern-matches to "danger." You're reviewing the logic, not auditing whether a four-word package name is real, because who does that?

3. The install runs code. On npm and pip, installing a package can execute a script automatically: a postinstall hook, a setup.py build step. The attacker's payload doesn't need you to import anything or call a function. install finished, so the code already ran.

4. Credentials leave the building. The payload reads what a build agent always has lying around: environment variables, ~/.aws/credentials, ~/.npmrc tokens, a GITHUB_TOKEN, .env files. It POSTs them to an attacker-controlled endpoint. From the outside it looks like a package fetching metadata during install. From the inside, your CI just handed a stranger the keys.

The whole thing is unnervingly quiet. There's no exploit, no CVE, no clever memory corruption. A developer trusted a name and ran the standard install command they run fifty times a day. That's the entire attack.

And it's not hypothetical that people fall for the trust step. Security researcher Bar Lanyado at Lasso Security noticed models repeatedly hallucinating a Python package called huggingface-cli. He registered an empty package under that exact name on PyPI as an experiment. Over the next three months it pulled more than 15,000 real downloads, and Alibaba's GraphTranslator project ended up recommending pip install huggingface-cli in its README, when the real tool installs with pip install -U "huggingface_hub[cli]". Lanyado's package was harmless on purpose. A slopsquatter's wouldn't be.

Same idea, four ecosystems, four different blast radii

The brief version is "it hits JavaScript, PHP, and Go alike." The accurate version is that each ecosystem hands the attacker a different amount of rope, and knowing the difference tells you where to spend your defense budget.

npm gives an attacker the most. Lifecycle scripts (preinstall, install, postinstall) run automatically on npm install. That's the classic vector, and it's exactly why the ecosystem is finally moving. pnpm v10 disabled dependency lifecycle scripts by default in early 2025, and npm followed: npm v12 turns off automatic script execution by default, announced in June 2026. Until you're on those versions, postinstall is a loaded gun pointed at your CI.

package.json (the malicious dependency)

{
  "name": "requests-oauth2-helper",
  "version": "1.0.3",
  "scripts": {
    "postinstall": "node ./collect.js"
  }
}

pip is close behind. A source distribution runs setup.py at install time to compute metadata and build, which means arbitrary code on pip install. A wheel (.whl) doesn't run install-time code the same way, which is why --only-binary is a real hardening lever, not a nicety.

# Refuse source builds; only accept prebuilt wheels
pip install --only-binary :all: requests-oauth2-helper

Composer is quietly the safest of the three, by design. Composer only executes scripts defined in the root package's composer.json. A dependency's own scripts block is ignored. So a slopsquatted Composer package can't hand you an automatic post-install-cmd, the way an npm package hands you a postinstall. The one caveat is plugins: a malicious Composer plugin can hook install events, which is why composer install --no-plugins --no-scripts exists for untrusted trees. The payload has to wait until your code actually calls into it, which is a meaningfully higher bar than "runs on install."

Go doesn't have install scripts at all, so the kill chain shifts. go get and go build don't run a package's arbitrary setup code the moment you add it. The malicious code in a slopsquatted Go module runs the first time your program executes it, via a package init() function on import, or during go test. Later, but not never.

Go adds its own twist through the module proxy. Socket found a backdoored typosquat of BoltDB, github.com/boltdb-go/bolt, that was uploaded in November 2021, cached by the Go module mirror, and then had its Git tag rewritten to clean code. The proxy kept serving the cached malicious version anyway. It went undetected for over three years. Caching that's meant to make builds reproducible also makes a poisoned version durable.

So the mental model isn't "one attack, three languages." It's: npm and pip fire on install, Composer waits for a plugin or a call, Go waits for execution and then remembers the bad version forever. A slopsquatter picks the ecosystem that gives them the earliest, quietest trigger.

Why your usual supply chain defenses don't catch this

Here's the uncomfortable part. Most of the controls you already run were built for a different threat model, and slopsquatting slips through the seams between them.

Lockfiles only help after the first install. A package-lock.json or composer.lock pins exact versions and hashes so a dependency can't silently change under you. That's great for a package you already vet and lock. But slopsquatting attacks the first install of a brand-new name. There's nothing in the lockfile yet, because you've never installed this thing. The AI just suggested it thirty seconds ago. The lockfile faithfully records whatever malicious version you first pulled, and now it's pinned. Lockfiles protect continuity, not first contact.

Scanners look for known-bad, and this is never-seen. A vulnerability scanner or a malware feed matches against packages someone has already flagged. A slopsquatted package registered yesterday, targeting a hallucination that only started recurring this quarter, has no CVE, no advisory, no reputation, no history. It's clean by absence. The scanner isn't broken; it's answering a different question. "Is this a known threat?" is not "is this a real package a human chose."

Typosquat detection keys on edit distance, and half these names don't resemble anything. The standard defense against typosquatting measures string similarity: how many edits to turn expres into express? Flag the near-misses. But remember the Levenshtein finding, nearly half of hallucinated names were highly dissimilar to any real package. requests-oauth2-helper isn't one edit away from a real thing. It's not a corruption of an existing name at all. It's a fresh invention that happens to sound plausible. There's no real neighbor to measure distance from, so the detector has nothing to trip on.

Put those three together and you see the shape of the gap. Every one of these defenses assumes the bad package either changed (lockfiles), was previously flagged (scanners), or mimics something real (typosquat detection). Slopsquatting is none of those. It's a genuinely new name, never seen, that doesn't resemble anything, chosen by a machine that sounds confident. The defenses aren't weak. They're aimed somewhere else.

What actually works: don't let a name into the repo on faith

The good news is that the fix isn't exotic. It's the same instinct that should govern any dependency, applied to a source you've started over-trusting. You don't need a new product category. You need to stop treating an AI's package suggestion as a citation.

Verify the package exists and is maintained before it touches your machine. Before you install anything a model handed you, look it up. Does it exist on the registry? How many downloads, how many versions, when was the last release, who publishes it, is there a repo behind it that a human clearly maintains? A slopsquatted package is usually days old with a suspiciously round download count and no history. Thirty seconds of looking kills most of these.

# npm: does it exist, who owns it, how old is it?
npm view requests-oauth2-helper

# PyPI: check the project page, release history, and maintainers
pip index versions requests-oauth2-helper

If the first command 404s, the model didn't find you a hidden gem. It made one up.

Disable install scripts by default. This single control neuters the loudest version of the kill chain. Turn automatic execution off and let real build steps be an explicit exception, not the default:

:::tabs
npm

# Kill lifecycle scripts globally; allow-list the rare package that needs one
npm config set ignore-scripts true

pnpm

# pnpm v10+ blocks dependency scripts by default.
# Approve only the ones you actually trust:
pnpm approve-builds

pip

# Prefer prebuilt wheels so setup.py never runs at install time
pip install --only-binary :all: <package>

composer

# Untrusted tree? No plugins, no scripts.
composer install --no-plugins --no-scripts

:::

Only about 2% of npm packages legitimately use install scripts, which is exactly why the ecosystem decided the sane default is off. You lose almost nothing and you close the door the payload was counting on.

Proxy everything through a private registry with an allowlist. A build agent should not be able to reach out to the public registry and pull whatever a model named. Put a proxy in front (Artifactory, Verdaccio, a private PyPI, Composer's Satis) and allow only packages that have been reviewed in. Now a hallucinated name doesn't fail after install, it fails before, because it was never approved. This is the control that scales, because it moves the decision from "did the developer notice" to "is this on the list."

Add a maturity delay for new versions. pnpm v11 shipped minimumReleaseAge, defaulting to 1440 minutes (24 hours), which refuses to install a package version until it's been public long enough for the community to catch obvious malware. A slopsquatted package racing to catch a fresh hallucination is exactly the thing a cooling-off window is good at stopping.

And the one rule under all the others: never let a dependency into the repo just because the AI suggested it. An AI package suggestion is a hypothesis, not a source. Treat it the way you'd treat a Stack Overflow answer from an account you've never seen: possibly right, worth checking, never trusted on sight. The whole attack hinges on that one moment of misplaced trust in step two. Verify the name and the attack has nowhere to stand.

The uncomfortable truth is that the model isn't going to stop doing this soon. Hallucination is a property of how these systems generate text, and a fake package name reads exactly like a real one from the inside. So the burden sits with you: the human who runs install. The name your assistant just gave you might be a real library, or it might be an attacker's package wearing a real library's name. The only way to tell them apart is to look before you install, and the whole point of slopsquatting is that you won't.

blocks.html_en: The scale first. A USENIX Security 2025 study, We Have a Package for You!, generated 576,000 code samples across 16 LLMs in Python and JavaScript and checked every package the models recommended. 19.7% of recommended packages didn't exist. That's not a rounding error at the edge of a benchmark. That's one in five. The study logged 205,474 distinct hallucinated package names. Commercial models were better behaved (at least 5.2% on average) and open-source models worse (at least 21.7%), but nobody was clean.

blocks.html_en: And it's not hypothetical that people fall for the trust step. Security researcher Bar Lanyado at Lasso Security noticed models repeatedly hallucinating a Python package called huggingface-cli. Over the next three months it pulled more than 15,000 real downloads, and Alibaba's GraphTranslator project ended up recommending pip install huggingface-cli in its README, when the real tool installs with pip install -U "huggingface_hub[cli]". blocks.html_en: npm gives an attacker the most. Lifecycle scripts (preinstall, install, postinstall) run automatically on npm install. blocks.html_en: Composer is quietly the safest of the three, by design. Composer only executes scripts defined in the root package's composer.json. A dependency's own scripts block is ignored. So a slopsquatted Composer package can't hand you an automatic post-install-cmd, the way an npm package hands you a postinstall. The one caveat is plugins: a malicious Composer plugin can hook install events, which is why composer install --no-plugins --no-scripts exists for untrusted trees. The payload has to wait until your code actually calls into it, which is a meaningfully higher bar than "runs on install."

错字抢注押注于你的错字。 盲目地押注于你的人工智能助手。 当模型创建一个不存在的包时，攻击者会注册该名称并等待安装运行。 这是杀伤链，为什么你通常的防御会错过它，以及实际上是什么通过 npm、Composer 和 pip 阻止它。

想象一下编码助理刚刚告诉你运行这个：

pip install requests-oauth2-helper

进入全屏模式 退出全屏模式

看起来不错。 您要求一种干净的方法将 OAuth2 令牌附加到您的请求调用，并且该名称读起来与执行此操作的包完全相同。 大小写是惯用的，连字符与生态系统相匹配，听起来像其他 50 个真正的 PyPI 助手。 所以你运行它。 测试通过。 你继续前进。

问题是，当模型学会建议它时，requests-oauth2-helper 从未存在过。 模型弥补了这一点。 如果攻击者注意到了，这个名字就不再是空的了。

这就是乱抢：一种供应链攻击，将抢注核心的人类拼写错误替换为机器幻觉。 该术语由 Python 软件基金会驻场开发人员 Seth Larson 创造，并由 Ecosyste.ms 的 Andrew Nesbitt 于 2025 年普及。 这是一个小主意，但却带来了可怕的后果：你不必再提出粗暴的要求了。 你的人工智能会板着脸自信地递给你一个假包裹，你会更相信它而不是你自己的打字错误。

误植需要你的错误。 这个没有。

抢注已经很老了。 你在express旁边注册了expres，在python-dateutil旁边注册了python-dateutl，然后等待某人的手指滑落。 它确实有效，但这是一场赔率微乎其微的数字游戏。 大多数人拼写表达都是正确的。 攻击者正在捕捞不这样做的一小部分人。

乱抢完全消除了对人为错误的依赖。 开发人员正确地逐个字符地输入名称，因为他们正在从他们现在比自己更信任的来源复制它：刚刚编写周围代码的助手。 这个错误已经由模型在上游犯下了，而人类正在忠实地重现它。

这是重要的转变。 在误植中，攻击者会猜测你的手指可能会滑入什么地方。 在乱蹲中，攻击者根本不会猜测。 他们大规模地读取模型实际输出的内容，并注册出现的名称。 该模型正在为他们进行目标选择。

为什么这有效：幻觉很常见，而且更糟糕的是，它们会重复出现

如果模型幻觉是罕见且随机的，那么乱蹲将是一个脚注。 注册一个假名字，永远等待，抓不到任何人。 这是一个真正的威胁，因为这两件事都不是真的。

先说规模。 USENIX Security 2025 研究“我们为您提供了一个包！”在 16 个法学硕士中使用 Python 和 JavaScript 生成了 576,000 个代码示例，并检查了模型推荐的每个包。 19.7% 的推荐包不存在。 这不是基准边缘的舍入误差。 那是五分之一。 该研究记录了 205,474 个不同的幻觉包名称。 商业模型表现较好（平均至少 5.2%），开源模型表现较差（至少 21.7%），但没有人是干净的。

如果每个幻觉都是一片独特的雪花，那么规模仍然是可控的，因为攻击者无法注册二十万个名字，并且不知道任何人会再次看到哪些名字。 致命的发现是幻觉是可以再现的。 研究人员接受了 500 个生成假包的提示，并将每个提示运行十次以上。 43%的幻觉包裹每次都会被退回。 58% 的人出现在不止一轮中。 只有 39% 的人再也没有出现过。

坐在那里。 这些构造中近一半是稳定的模型行为，而不是噪声。 这完全颠覆了经济学。 攻击者不需要注册所有内容。 他们挖掘模型输出，保留重复出现的名称，并注册粘性名称。 再现性就是勘察。 该模型一遍又一遍地告诉他们，未来的开发人员最有可能使用哪个假名字。

警告 这些名称甚至不必看起来像真正的包。 使用 Levenshtein 距离，同一研究发现只有 13% 的幻觉名字是真实名字的简单拼写错误。 大约 38% 具有中等相似性，近一半则高度不同：完全是捏造的，但在其周围的代码背景下仍然可信。 最后一个桶是直接通过仿冒域名检测的桶，我们将回到原因。

杀戮链，一步一步

这些都不是理论上的。 这是一个干净、可重复的序列，每个链接都是您在正常工作日中看到的。

1. 该模型建议进口。 你要求一个功能。 助手编写代码并找到适合问题形状的依赖项。 它发出一个名字。 这个名字是发明出来的，但它是符合语法的：正确的生态系统惯例、正确的外壳、正确的“听起来像是存在的东西”能量。

2. 您信任它，因为它的名字很合适。 这是承重步骤，是心理上的，而不是技术上的。 自信的人工智能输出会滑过你的防线，就像自信的高级工程师的公关一样。 这个名字很地道。 它与“危险”没有任何模式匹配。 您正在审查逻辑，而不是审核四字包名称是否真实，因为谁会这样做？

3. 安装运行代码。 在 npm 和 pip 上，安装包可以自动执行脚本：postinstall 挂钩、setup.py 构建步骤。 攻击者的有效负载不需要您导入任何内容或调用函数。 安装完成，因此代码已经运行。

4. 凭证离开大楼。 有效负载读取构建代理始终存在的内容：环境变量、~/.aws/credentials、~/.npmrc 令牌、GITHUB_TOKEN、.env 文件。 它将它们发布到攻击者控制的端点。 从外部看，它看起来像是一个在安装过程中获取元数据的包。 从内部来看，你的 CI 刚刚把钥匙交给了一个陌生人。

整个事情安静得令人不安。 没有漏洞利用，没有 CVE，也没有巧妙的内存损坏。 开发人员信任某个名称并运行他们每天运行五十次的标准安装命令。 这就是整个攻击过程。

这并不是假设人们会陷入信任步骤。 Lasso Security 的安全研究员 Bar Lanyado 注意到模型反复产生一个名为 Huggingface-cli 的 Python 包的幻觉。 他在 PyPI 上以该名称注册了一个空包作为实验。 在接下来的三个月里，它获得了超过 15,000 次实际下载，阿里巴巴的 GraphTranslator 项目最终在其 README 中推荐了 pip install Huggingface-cli，而真正的工具是通过 pip install -U "huggingface_hub[cli]" 安装的。 兰亚多的包裹是故意无害的。 擅自占地者就不会这样。

相同的想法，四种生态系统，四种不同的爆炸半径

简短的版本是“它同样适用于 JavaScript、PHP 和 Go”。 准确的版本是，每个生态系统为攻击者提供了不同数量的绳索，了解差异可以告诉您将防御预算花在哪里。

npm 给攻击者带来的好处最多。 生命周期脚本（安装前、安装、安装后）在 npm install 上自动运行。 这是经典的向量，这正是生态系统最终移动的原因。 pnpm v10 在 2025 年初默认禁用依赖生命周期脚本，npm 紧随其后：npm v12 默认关闭自动脚本执行，于 2026 年 6 月宣布。 在您使用这些版本之前，安装后就像一把上了膛的枪指向您的 CI。

package.json（恶意依赖项）

{
  "name": "requests-oauth2-helper",
  "version": "1.0.3",
  "scripts": {
    "postinstall": "node ./collect.js"
  }
}

进入全屏模式 退出全屏模式

pip 紧随其后。 源发行版在安装时运行 setup.py 来计算元数据和构建，这意味着 pip install 上的任意代码。 轮子 (.whl) 不会以相同的方式运行安装时代码，这就是为什么 --only-binary 是一个真正的强化杠杆，而不是一个细节。

# Refuse source builds; only accept prebuilt wheels
pip install --only-binary :all: requests-oauth2-helper

进入全屏模式 退出全屏模式

从设计上来说，Composer 无疑是三者中最安全的。 Composer 仅执行根包的composer.json 中定义的脚本。 依赖项自己的脚本块将被忽略。 因此，一个草率的 Composer 软件包无法为您提供自动的安装后 cmd，就像 npm 软件包为您提供安装后的方式一样。 需要注意的是插件：恶意 Composer 插件可以挂钩安装事件，这就是为什么不可信树存在composer install --no-plugins --no-scripts 的原因。 有效负载必须等到您的代码实际调用它，这比“安装时运行”要高得多。

Go 根本没有安装脚本，因此杀伤链发生了变化。 go get 和 go build 在添加包时不会运行包的任意设置代码。 恶意的 Go 模块中的恶意代码会在程序第一次执行时运行，通过导入时的包 init() 函数或在 go 测试期间运行。 后来，但并非永远。

Go 通过模块代理添加了自己的特色。 Socket 发现了 BoltDB 的后门误植，github.com/boltdb-go/bolt，于 2021 年 11 月上传，由 Go 模块镜像缓存，然后将其 Git 标签重写为干净的代码。 代理无论如何都会继续提供缓存的恶意版本。 三年多来，它一直未被发现。 缓存旨在使构建可重现，同时也使中毒版本变得持久。

因此，心理模型不是“一次攻击，三种语言”。 它是：npm 和 pip 在安装时触发，Composer 等待插件或调用，Go 等待执行，然后永远记住错误的版本。 擅自占地者会选择最早、最安静的触发因素的生态系统。

为什么您通常的供应链防御措施无法捕捉到这一点

这是不舒服的部分。 您已经运行的大多数控件都是针对不同的威胁模型而构建的，而擅自抢注会穿过它们之间的缝隙。

锁定文件仅在首次安装后才有帮助。 package-lock.json 或composer.lock 固定精确的版本和哈希值，因此依赖项无法在您的控制下悄然更改。 这对于您已经审查并锁定的包裹来说非常有用。 但擅自抢注会攻击全新名称的首次安装。 锁定文件中还没有任何内容，因为您从未安装过这个东西。 AI 在三十秒前刚刚提出建议。 锁定文件忠实地记录了您第一次提取的任何恶意版本，现在它已被固定。 锁定文件保护连续性，而不是第一次接触。

扫描仪会寻找已知的不良行为，但这是从未见过的。 漏洞扫描程序或恶意软件源与某人已标记的软件包进行匹配。 昨天注册的一个草率的包裹，针对的是本季度才开始出现的幻觉，没有 CVE，没有咨询，没有声誉，没有历史。 不在场就干净了。 扫描仪没有坏；它正在回答一个不同的问题。 “这是已知的威胁吗？” 不是“这是人类选择的真正的包裹吗？”

编辑距离上的误植检测键，其中一半的名称与任何东西都不相似。 针对拼写错误的标准防御措施是衡量字符串相似性：需要进行多少次编辑才能将表达式转换为表达式？ 标记未遂事件。 但请记住 Levenshtein 的发现，近一半的幻觉名称与任何真实的包裹都非常不同。 requests-oauth2-helper 与真实的东西相差不远。 这根本不是对现有名称的破坏。 这是一项听起来似乎合理的新鲜发明。 没有真正的邻居可以测量距离，因此探测器没有什么可以绊倒的。

将这三者放在一起，您就可以看到间隙的形状。 这些防御措施中的每一种都假设坏包要么被更改（锁定文件），要么先前被标记（扫描程序），要么模仿真实的东西（误植检测）。 乱蹲都不是这些。 这是一个真正的新名字，从未见过，与任何东西都不相似，是由一台听起来很自信的机器选择的。 防御力并不弱。 他们的目标是其他地方。

实际有效的方法：不要凭信心将名字放入存储库中

好消息是这个修复方法并不陌生。 同样的本能应该控制任何依赖性，应用于您已经开始过度信任的来源。 您不需要新的产品类别。 你需要停止将人工智能的包裹建议视为引文。

在接触您的机器之前验证该包是否存在并得到维护。 在安装模型交给你的任何东西之前，先查一下。 它存在于注册表中吗？ 有多少次下载，有多少个版本，最后一次发布是什么时候，谁发布的，背后是否有人类明确维护的存储库？ 乱七八糟的软件包通常已经存在几天了，下载次数可疑，而且没有历史记录。 三十秒的观察就能杀死大部分人。

# npm: does it exist, who owns it, how old is it?
npm view requests-oauth2-helper

# PyPI: check the project page, release history, and maintainers
pip index versions requests-oauth2-helper

如果第一个命令出现 404s，则模型没有为您找到隐藏的宝石。 这是编造出来的。

默认情况下禁用安装脚本。 这个单一控制可以消除杀伤链中最响亮的版本。 关闭自动执行并让真正的构建步骤成为显式异常，而不是默认情况：

:::标签 npm

# Kill lifecycle scripts globally; allow-list the rare package that needs one
npm config set ignore-scripts true

进入全屏模式 退出全屏模式

pnpm

# pnpm v10+ blocks dependency scripts by default.
# Approve only the ones you actually trust:
pnpm approve-builds

进入全屏模式 退出全屏模式

pip

# Prefer prebuilt wheels so setup.py never runs at install time
pip install --only-binary :all: <package>

进入全屏模式 退出全屏模式

作曲家

# Untrusted tree? No plugins, no scripts.
composer install --no-plugins --no-scripts

进入全屏模式 退出全屏模式

:::

只有大约 2% 的 npm 包合法地使用安装脚本，这正是生态系统决定关闭合理默认值的原因。 你几乎没有损失任何东西，并且你关上了有效载荷所指望的门。

通过带有白名单的私有注册表代理所有内容。 构建代理不应该能够访问公共注册表并提取任何命名的模型。 将代理放在前面（Artifactory、Verdaccio、私有 PyPI、Composer 的 Satis）并仅允许已审核的包。 现在，幻觉名称在安装后不会失败，它之前会失败，因为它从未被批准。 这是可扩展的控件，因为它将决策从“开发人员是否注意到”转移到“这个是否在列表中”。

为新版本添加成熟延迟。 pnpm v11 提供了最小发布期限，默认为 1440 分钟（24 小时），它拒绝安装软件包版本，直到它公开足够长的时间以使社区能够捕获明显的恶意软件。 一个乱七八糟的包裹竞相捕捉新的幻觉，这正是冷静窗口最擅长阻止的事情。

所有其他规则中的一条规则是：永远不要仅仅因为人工智能建议就将依赖项放入存储库中。 AI 包建议只是一种假设，而不是来源。 就像对待来自您从未见过的帐户的 Stack Overflow 答案一样：可能是正确的，值得检查，但从不可信。 整个攻击取决于第二步中错误信任的那一刻。 验证名字，攻击无立足之地。

令人不安的事实是，该模型不会很快停止这样做。 幻觉是这些系统生成文本的一种属性，假包名称从内部读起来与真实包名称完全相同。 因此，负担由您承担：运行安装的人员。 您的助手刚刚给您提供的名称可能是一个真正的库，也可能是攻击者使用真实库名称的包。 区分它们的唯一方法是在安装之前进行查看，而乱抢的全部意义在于您不会这样做。
